newsitem.title: SPAIN: Truck strike tapers off in Spain, foreigners hit.
newsitem.headline: Truck strike tapers off in Spain, foreigners hit.

text.p: A Spanish truckers' strike that has dragged on for more than two weeks appeared Tuesday to be tapering off but the effect on Spanish suppliers to European car makers was still being felt.
The government guaranteed the security of traffic and provided escorts through picketed areas where requested, saying negative effects had been exaggerated by media hype.

"From the first moment, the government has said that there was a radical and violent minority manipulating the facts that appear in the media," Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar told a news conference in The Hague.
Carmakers have been forced to cut back production for lack of parts, but most effects on the Spanish economy are left over from last week's bigger-scale disruptions.
Two major German carmakers announced a new round of production stoppages affecting thousands more workers.
Adam Opel AG, the German unit of General Motors Corp., said the Spanish strike has now affected about 20,000 members of its workforce and has prevented the production of some 11,000 vehicles.

Volkswagen AG, Europe's largest carmaker, said it would stop all production of its Polo model at the main Wolfsburg plant as of Tuesday night, preventing production of about 1,000 vehicles a day and affecting about 3,500 workers.
Production at car assembly plants was disrupted across Portugal on Tuesday and about 100 British trucks were stuck in the Basque region.
Spanish trade unions accused the Madrid administration of being in no hurry to resolve the dispute, which hinges on truckers' demands for earlier retirement and lower fuel costs.
The government denied this was the case, saying it had been willing to resolve the conflict from the outset. Moreover, talks were making progress.

"We've had something of an approximation of views in some respects, and (the union is) exaggerating the implications of the talks so far. They know if we gave in to their demands it would mean the bankruptcy of the social security system," a Development Ministry spokesman said.
The main bone of contention is the strikers' demand for retirement at 60 instead of 65, maintaining pension allowances.
While negotiations continued late on Tuesday, the government said it was guaranteeing free traffic movement nationwide and there were only isolated incidents of violence.
Some 50 people, mostly picketers or protesters blocking highways with burning tyres, were arrested after clashes with police or non-striking truck drivers, police said.
The Interior Ministry said there was no area that was gravely damaged by the stoppage, including the northern region which was badly hit last week.
While the government insisted it was business as usual, carmaker stoppages prompted fears that foreigners might take their business elsewhere.

But corporate officials seemed unruffled. A General Motors official said the U.S. auto giant, which produces the Opel and Vauxhall brands in Europe, was not contemplating changing its supplier contracts in Spain.
"There's always the possibility of some work stoppage in any European country. There can be a strike anywhere. Those kinds of things are part and parcel of democratic processes," he said.
